table.answer: The claim that drinking water with lemon can prevent COVID-19 is false based on the evidence obtained. [E7] The National Academies states: “Lemon juice will not prevent or cure a COVID-19 infection, no matter what is mixed with it.” [E7] This guidance was last updated April 22, 2020, after the claim date of March 8, 2020; what guidance was available on that earlier date was not established. [E7] The assessment concerns COVID-19 prevention and relies on published scientific guidance, not an independently examined clinical trial of lemon water. [E7]

The claim that Mel Gibson said “The only reason liberals hate Trump is they hate God” is not verifiable from the evidence obtained: two retrieved blogs attribute it to him, but no authenticated recording, original interview or direct statement was obtained.[E1][E2] Separate reporting documents Gibson expressing support for Trump, but does not authenticate this quotation.[E4] The evidence therefore supports an unverified attribution, not a definitive finding that the quotation was fabricated.[E1][E2]

The full claim is not verifiable from the evidence obtained: the Iraq portion has support, but Biden’s support for wars in Serbia, Syria, and Libya remains unestablished.[E1][E4]

Iraq: C-SPAN identifies a clip as Biden voting for the 2002 authorization to use military force against Iraq; this supports the claim’s Iraq portion, although the assessment relies on the page’s identification rather than an independently checked Senate roll call.[E1]

Syria: CNN reports that Biden demanded accountability for the alleged 2013 chemical attack, but those remarks do not establish that he supported military strikes; readiness to execute military options was attributed to Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel, conditional on President Obama’s order.[E4]

Serbia and Libya: Biden’s support for military intervention is not determinable from the obtained evidence; the specific interventions, dates, and scope of his support or opposition across these three countries remain unverified.[E4]

The claim is not verifiable as stated: the evidence supports similar remarks in a Mark Pocan interview, but does not establish a tweet on January 16, 2020 or the exact wording claimed. [E4] The Metro Weekly interview page dates to April 6, 2017, with an archive capture that same day. [E5] The interview attributes an Amazon distribution center advertising up to $12.75 an hour to Pocan, but does not establish the claimed wording about his last visit. [E4] Its generational comparison is conditional—children earning less than their parents did three decades earlier—rather than the categorical assertion that their parents earned that amount. [E4] The advertised wage, applicable facility and jobs, and historical parental wages were not independently verified; the evidence also does not resolve whether the comparison uses nominal or inflation-adjusted dollars. [E4]

The claim that U.S. homeowners insurance had increased by 50% as of January 3, 2020 is not verifiable from the evidence obtained. [E1][E8]
ValuePenguin’s June 4, 2020 release reported a 59% increase over the preceding decade, which does not establish the claimed increase by January 3, 2020. [E1]
The report of increases exceeding 50% concerned two Florida insurers seeking approval for increases on some policies, not an implemented nationwide increase; that article was published in February 2024. [E8][E10]
These differences in timing, geography and measurement leave the claim unsupported, rather than proven false. [E1][E8][E10]

The claim is not verifiable from the evidence obtained. The CNN coverage describes Trump's September 2019 rally in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, including remarks about Obama. [E1] Whether Trump said the quoted words on August 15, 2019, their context, and whether Obama left him 138 judicial vacancies remain undetermined.

The claim that the US, Russia, Israel and France approved Biafra’s separation from Nigeria as of 2019-05-31 is not verifiable from the evidence obtained.[E3]
The historical account examined describes limited French military support, covert Israeli assistance and US neutrality with humanitarian relief during the Nigerian Civil War, which do not establish approval of secession in 2019.[E3]
The NewsVerifierAfrica article concerns a separate October 27, 2025 allegation about Burkina Faso and Russia, while the BBC article concerns later US relations with Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger; neither establishes the claimed May 2019 approval.[E1][E5]
Relevant May 2019 approval statements or actions by the four countries, their speakers, dates, locations and original sources—including Russia’s position on the alleged approval—were not established in the investigation.[E3]

The claim is accurate according to the reporting obtained: Nigeria was described as having the world’s highest number of out-of-school children, which also supports the ranking within sub-Saharan Africa.[E6][E12] Global Citizen attributed an estimate of 13.2 million to a UNICEF survey; Vanguard separately reported a federal government estimate of 10.5 million and the same global ranking.[E6][E12] This conclusion concerns the absolute number of children, not the percentage out of school.[E6][E12] The underlying survey, a contemporaneous country-by-country comparison, and equivalent age coverage and reference periods for the two estimates were not independently verified, so an exact count applicable on the claim date remains unestablished.[E6][E12]

The claim is not verifiable from the evidence obtained. [E1] The Washington Post reported that Trump’s campaign announced raising more than $30 million in the first three months of 2019, but this dollar total does not establish the percentage of contributions of $200 or less or the number of distinct small donors. [E1] Trump’s 2025 personal financial disclosure concerns personal finances rather than first-quarter 2019 campaign contributions; it cannot establish the contribution counts, committee coverage or counting conventions needed to determine the claimed percentage. [E4] The characterization of “immense grassroots support” is therefore also not established by the obtained fundraising evidence. [E1]

The claim is not verifiable from the evidence obtained: none establishes all three totals or attributes them to BLM as of July 25, 2020. [E2][E3][E6]

Police injuries: The New York Post reported 292 injured NYPD officers, citing police; this local count does not verify 1,000 nationwide or establish that BLM caused those injuries. [E2]

Deaths: LegalHelp reports at least 25 deaths associated with the protests, which neither verifies 36 people killed by BLM nor disproves that number, since it is a lower bound with no established attribution. [E3]

Damage: The obtained estimates concern $1 billion to $2 billion in insured losses, not total damage, so they neither substantiate nor directly disprove the $8 billion claim. [E3][E6]

The Hill report was published September 16, 2020, after the claim date; the evidence does not establish the claimed nationwide totals by July 25. [E6][E8]

The claim that the Green New Deal would eliminate air travel is misleading based on the evidence obtained: contemporary reporting distinguishes the resolution from accompanying FAQs and reports that Ocasio-Cortez disowned FAQ statements that went beyond the resolution. [E4] Markey and Ocasio-Cortez introduced the resolution on February 7, 2019; the official announcement establishes a proposal, not an implemented policy eliminating air travel. [E1] The original FAQ wording and full legislative text were not directly verified for this assessment, and the evidence does not establish the eventual effects of implementation. [E4]

The claim is not verifiable from the evidence obtained; the examined sources establish neither its accuracy nor its falsity. [E1][E3][E2] Kenya’s 2013 electricity connection total, whether it counts people, households or customer connections, and its reference date and geographic coverage cannot be determined from the examined sources. [E1][E3]

The claim is not verifiable from the evidence obtained: individual historical milestones do not establish that every outbreak in the unidentified list originated in China. [E3][E5][E2]

For 1957, a historical review places influenza emergence in China that winter and a subsequent major epidemic in Hong Kong in April. [E3] CDC describes H2N2 emerging in East Asia in February 1957. [E4]

For 1968, CDC identifies H3N2 as triggering the pandemic and replacing H2N2, but this evidence does not establish its geographic origin. [E5]

For 1997, CDC identifies the first human H5N1 infection in Hong Kong; this does not establish the virus’s ultimate origin. [E2]

The original list’s membership, its connection to that later article, an entry-by-entry verdict, and the origin of the referenced 2003 event remain undetermined; outbreak emergence and first identified human infection must not be equated with ultimate viral origin. [E7][E3][E5][E2]

The title accurately attributes the statement to Clinton, but the claim that no lives were lost is not verifiable from the evidence obtained.[E11][E15] The video’s speech concerns Libya’s transition and contrasts it with Syria; The Hill describes her statement as referring to American lives during involvement in deposing Gadhafi, rather than all deaths in Libya.[E11][E15] The sampled pictures show a televised town hall, with MSNBC branding, and provide no evidence of casualties in Libya.[E5][E9][E12] The supplied March 15 posting date was not independently verified.[E16] The casualty total and the precise personnel, operations and period encompassed by her statement remain unverified, so the supported conclusion concerns attribution and context only.[E11][E15]

The full claim is not verifiable from the evidence, although external reporting supports the broader allegation that law enforcement slashed parked-car tires during the Minneapolis protests.[E14][E16] CBS News identifies Minnesota State Patrol troopers as admitting to deflating tires; this does not establish that Minneapolis Police Department officers damaged the vehicles in this video.[E15]

The supplied images show visibly deflated tires on several vehicles, but do not establish visible cuts, who caused the damage, which vehicle was rented, or whether every tire on every car was affected.[E4][E5][E8][E10] The narrator’s speech and relevant on-screen wording were not verified, so what the video says cannot be determined from the examined visual evidence.[E12]

The May 31, 2020 posting date remains unverified; the candidate Global News broadcast is dated June 1, 2020, and its metadata does not establish a connection to this particular footage.[E18] Thus, the rental-car identification, responsible agency, and universal “every tire” allegation remain undetermined, rather than disproved.[E14][E15][E16]

The claim is misleading on the evidence obtained: it turns a political allegation into a categorical prediction that Biden would abolish the Second Amendment. [E11][E18]

The video's speech alleges that “they are going to terminate, in my opinion, or essentially do the same thing, your Second Amendment”; the transcript neither names Biden nor presents a statement by him. [E11] The imagery shows a seated man holding a telephone receiver with a campaign-style banner, rather than evidence of Biden announcing such a policy. [E13]

The external CNN report records Biden's pledge to pursue an assault-weapons ban if elected, which does not establish a pledge to abolish the Second Amendment. [E18]

This conclusion is limited to the allegation and the reported proposal: Biden's complete position as of July 31, 2020, the supplied posting date, and the video's full original context were not independently verified, and the original campaign policy document was not obtained. [E11][E18]
